newsitem.title: USA: Western, KCPL bury hatchet in $2 bln merger.
newsitem.headline: Western, KCPL bury hatchet in $2 bln merger.

text.p: Western Resources and Kansas City Power and Light Co agreed to a $2 billion merger Friday, turning what started as a bitter unsolicited takeover into a seemingly amicable agreement that will create a Midwestern electric and natural gas powerhouse.

The merger, if approved by shareholders of both companies and by regulators, will create a company with more than two million security and energy customers, $9.5 billion in assets, $3 billion in annual revenues and more than 8,000 megawatts of electric generation resources.

In announcing the agreement, Western Chairman and CEO John Hayes and KC Power CEO Drue Jennings said they had buried the hatchet in the saga that began last April when Western launched its takeover bid and eventually scuttled KC Power's friendly merger pact with UtiliCorp United Inc.

"The process of merging our companies has been long and, at times, trying. Today, we are putting the past behind us and we are ready to plan our future," Hayes told reporters in a teleconference after the deal was announced.
"With this combination, we rapidly move forward to creating one of the nation's premier providers of security and energy products and services," Hayes said.
Analysts believe the merger will create the nation's 34th largest utility, and one that is better poised to compete as the U.S. utility business is deregulated.
In separate meetings, the two companies' boards of directors approved a definitive merger agreement that provides for a tax-free, stock-for-stock transaction valued at about $2 billion.

Hayes will remain chairman and chief executive officer of Topeka, Kansas-based Western Resources. Jennings will become vice chairman of Western's board and will be responsible for electric utility operations of the combined company upon completion of the merger.

Jennings said the turning point in negotiations came when Western began to reshape itself as more than just an electric utility by buying the monitored security business of Westinghouse Electric Corp and by launching an unsolicited bid for electronic security giant ADT Ltd.
"KCPL has long recognized that to thrive in this increasingly competitive environment, we needed to have significantly enhanced scale and resources," Hayes said.

"Frankly, at the time we began our merger discussions with UtiliCorp, Western Resources appeared to us to be quite a traditional utility company," Jennings said. "But things have changed and they've changed dramatically.
Jennings said the new company would commit to no employee layoffs, and to long-range cost savings of $1 billion over the next 10 years.
"Anyone who wants to stay with the new company will have an opportunity to do so," Hayes said.

Hayes said he thought the proposed merger would not have any difficulty meeting the new tougher merger guidelines adopted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. He said he expected to receive regulatory approval of the merger within 12 months.
Western still has outstanding a $3.5 billion hostile bid for ADT, in which it already owns a 27.1 percent stake.
